entries.title: Cubs 3B Alex Bregman's team-bonding trip to Churchill Downs is a rousing success
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — For the Cubs’ off day Thursday, third baseman and race-horse owner Alex Bregman helped organize a team trip to Churchill Downs. It ended up being a wonderful bonding experience, and he made a little bit of money, to boot.</p><p>Bregman’s horse Act of Parliament won his first race in four career starts, taking a maiden claiming race by less than a length in front of the whole team — including reliever Ryan Rolison, who was dressed as a horse. More on that later.</p><p>The trip had been planned for a month. Within that time, Bregman Family Racing bought Act of Parliament, who went to post in the final race of the night. The atmosphere at the track was far from what it is on Derby Day, at least until the dark bay colt rallied to win in an 11-horse field.</p><p>The Cubs celebrated wildly in the winner’s circle and hoisted jockey Axel Concepcion as though he had hit a walk-off home run. Act of Parliament paid out $8.68 off a $2 bet to win, and he earned Bregman, who has raced horses since 2022, $27,108 of the $48,000 purse. Act of Parliament got claimed, though, likely ending his time in Bregman’s stable.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr"><a href="https://x.com/a_concepcion16?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@a_concepcion16</a> gets it done for <a href="https://x.com/ABREG_1?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@ABREG_1</a> and the <a href="https://x.com/Cubs?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Cubs</a> ✅ <a href="https://t.co/57bX3rWY1A">pic.twitter.com/57bX3rWY1A</a></p>— Churchill Downs (@ChurchillDowns) <a href="https://x.com/ChurchillDowns/status/2100762275028074818?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>But the payout wasn’t the point of the trip. The Cubs flew into Louisville, Kentucky, on Thursday, the day before opening a three-game series against the Reds about 100 miles away, for the purpose of coming together away from baseball at a pressure-packed time of the season.</p><p>“It was a great time,” Bregman said. “We had all the guys out there. It was a lot of fun to be able to share that experience with them. Just being around the group this time of year is super important, just building a camaraderie.”</p><p>Bregman shared much of the experience on Instagram. He showed a video of center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong petting Act of Parliament before the race with the caption, “PCA pep talk we couldn't lose.”</p><p>“I just think it’s good that you get the whole group together, having fun,” said Bregman, who has had plenty of fun himself since the All-Star break, entering Friday with a 1.007 OPS and 17 home runs in 56 games. “It’s what it’s all about, building that team chemistry. That was probably a core memory for me right there doing it with this group of guys.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Off day W courtesy of <a href="https://x.com/ABREG_1?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@ABREG_1</a>’s horse at <a href="https://x.com/ChurchillDowns?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@ChurchillDowns</a>. 🐎 <a href="https://t.co/jC40JhFvQG">pic.twitter.com/jC40JhFvQG</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2100789335482155222?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>That includes Rolison, who got stuck wearing a silly horse costume for opening his big mouth in a pitchers meeting a month ago. Manager Craig Counsell was there, and he revealed the plan for the off day. Some veterans said the trip would be a good time a rookie dress-up day.</p><p>“Thank God I don’t have to do that anymore, because I had to do it last year,” Rolison said.</p><p>Replied Counsell: “You don’t get to decide when you’re a rookie.”</p><p>So even with more than two years of service time, Rolison was a rookie again.</p><p>“It was good fun,” he said. “I’m a big personality in the clubhouse. So they gave me the horse, and everyone else was jockeys. I embraced it.”</p><p>And the Cubs embraced each other, which is a good sign for a team looking to get on a roll before the posteason. They entered Friday with their magic number for a playoff spot at four, meaning they could have it wrapped up this weekend.</p><p>When they walked into the visitor’s clubhouse at Great American Ballpark, they were met by wet carpet and an odor of beer and champagne, remnants of the Dodgers’ celebration for winning yet another division title Thursday. Could that smell of victory inspire the Cubs this weekend?</p><p>“It just smells in there, to be honest with you,” Counsell said.</p><p>It sounds like the Cubs will have to channel their joy from Churchill toward their playoff push.</p><p>“What are the chances, we plan this trip, and Bregman buys a horse, and it’s the last race of the night and the horse wins?” Rolison said. “You can’t script it out any better. It was a great team-bonding off day.”</p>

entries.title: Nazareth's defense dominates Providence, which loses its first game after firing Tyler Plantz
entries.summary: <p>Two teams facing a midseason gut-check met up on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/17/high-school-football-scores-week-5" >Friday</a> in LaGrange Park.</p><p>No. 5 Providence spent the past week in a media firestorm after the school <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/14/tyler-plantz-providence-football-fired" >fired head coach Tyler Plantz</a>. The unusual mid-season <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/13/providence-fires-football-coach-tyler-plantz" >coaching change</a> caught the attention of casual sports fans and the local television media.</p><p>For Nazareth, the problems this season have all been on the field. The Roadrunners were highly touted in the preseason but lost three of their first four games. The defeats were to good teams, and Nazareth is missing several of its top players to injuries, but the season risked heading down a negative path with another loss.</p><p>“Our two senior captains have been injured, and we have had a lot of adversity against us,” Nazareth receiver Jackson Flickenger said. “We had meetings all this week about staying together, and we took that super seriously.”</p><p>The No. 22 Roadrunners dominated defensively and pulled out a 17-7 victory. It was Providence's first loss of the season, now helmed by interim head coach Adam Nissen, previously the team’s offensive coordinator.</p><p>Nissen acknowledged before the game that a loss was likely to fan the flames of controversy that started on Sunday when Providence announced Plantz’s firing. But he isn’t worried about how his team will handle the defeat internally.</p><p>“Our senior group is awesome,” Nissen said. “I have no doubt we will bounce back. We will watch some film and get ready. We will be ready next week.”</p><p>The Celtics (4-1) had a chance to cut the deficit to one possession when they recovered an onside kick with 8:40 left, trailing 17-7.</p><p>But junior defensive lineman John Bukovac stepped up with a big sack on the next play. And junior linebacker Harry Keenan grabbed an interception on fourth down with just more than a minute to play that sealed the win.</p><p>“We had to stay locked in as a team and trust each other and get it done,” Keenan said.</p><p>Sean Trayser and Henry Walz had interceptions for Nazareth in the first half.</p><p>“The defense was excellent,” Roadrunners coach Tim Racki said. “Especially with the weapons Providence has. Their running game is lethal.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Second INT of the game for Nazareth. Henry Walz grabs the tipped pass. <br><br>Roadrunners and Providence scoreless in the 2Q. <a href="https://t.co/I5XaGiCYQn">pic.twitter.com/I5XaGiCYQn</a></p>— Michael O'Brien (@michaelsobrien) <a href="https://x.com/michaelsobrien/status/2101093396979097924?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>But Nazareth’s running game stole the show. Charles Calhoun put the Roadrunners (2-3) ahead 17-0 with a six-yard TD run to cap off a drive that sucked up most of the third quarter.</p><p>“That was like a 10-minute drive,” Calhoun said. “I could feel it. We were on a roll. Once we get on a high, there is no taking us down.”</p><p>Calhoun had 24 carries for 103 yards, and Jack Parisi added 14 carries for 77 yards.</p><p>Nazareth quarterback JJ Chapman was 7-for-16 passing for 89 yards. He threw a 34-yard touchdown pass to Charles Heck late in the first half. Flickenger had five catches for 42 yards.</p><p>“We really came to play a complete football game,” Racki said. “And that is hard to do after an emotional loss last week. Our kids had an edge all week.”</p><p>Providence running back Broden Mackert had 17 carries for 123 yards and one touchdown. Celtics quarterback Dominic Vita went 13 of 20 for 90 yards with three interceptions.</p><p>“We definitely knew they had been through some adversity this week with their coach being fired,” Calhoun said. “We came out hard. We knew it would be a game to fight for and we wanted to use that to our advantage.”</p><p>Nazareth limited media access to the game, and no television cameras or independent videographers were present.</p><p>Otherwise, it was business as usual for Providence despite all the controversy around Plantz’s firing. A handful of Celtics fans in the crowd wore white T-shirts that read “We support coach Plantz.”</p><p>“We left too many plays on the field,” Nissen, who was previously a head coach at St. Laurence, said. “A couple turnovers; didn’t execute like we normally do. We had a good week of practice and were pretty locked in on what we were trying to do. We had the opportunities at the end of the game; we just couldn’t capitalize on it.”</p>

entries.title: Gaby Domercant looking forward to next adventure at DePaul Prep
entries.summary: <p>For pretty much her whole life, Gaby Domercant has embraced new adventures.</p><p>A couple of more are on tap.</p><p>After sitting out last season following her transfer from Young, Domercant is preparing for her senior basketball season at DePaul Prep. And the season after that, she’ll be off to play college ball at Iona after recently committing to the Gaels.</p><p>‘‘I really prayed about it a lot and I really connected with the staff on my visit,’’ Domercant told the Sun-Times. ‘‘They have a lot of dexperience, so that was something I really valued. And they’ve been winning. They’ve been super-successful in the [Metro] conference already.’’</p><p>Iona was one of 17 Division I scholarship offers for Domercant, a 5-9 guard. Through the recruiting process, she had the advice of her parents, both of whom were Division I athletes. Dad Henry is now a Bulls assistant after playing at Naperville North and Eastern Illinois before a long career overseas. Mom Alexandra played volleyball at Eastern Illinois.</p><p>‘‘My dad thought I was going into the volleyball pipeline . . . but I just fell in love with basketball and he couldn’t keep me away,’’ Domercant said jokingly.</p><p>That love for the game grew when Domercant was living in Russia, Turkey and Italy during her dad’s playing days.</p><p>‘‘Basketball has taken our family all over the world,’’ she said. ‘‘I was super-grateful for all of those experiences.’’</p><p>That globetrotting has given her a perspective that’s rare for a teenager.</p><p>‘‘I remember Turkey the most because I went to grade school there,’’ Domercant said. ‘‘My best friend was Turkish. I went to an English preschool, [and] we would go on all these crazy field trips. . . . All of those kids were learning English, so we were able to communicate a little bit.’’</p><p>Now she’s ready to embark on another adventure at DePaul Prep.</p><p>The Rams went 22-7 and reached a Class 4A regional final last season, but they graduated two Division I recruits in 6-2 Grace Lee (Boston University), the program’s career scoring leader, and 6-2 Kaitlin Totaro (Loyola-Maryland).</p><p>Domercant has expanded her skills since the last time she played high school basketball as a sophomore at Young in 2024-25.</p><p>‘‘I know a lot of people know me as someone who would stand there and shoot,’’ she said. ‘‘I’m trying to expand my game to do other things and contribute in other ways.’’</p><p>DePaul coach Corey Morgan said he is eager for others to see this new version of Domercant, who isn’t going to completely change her identity.</p><p>‘‘She’s an amazing shooter, a dynamic scorer,’’ Morgan told the Sun-Times. ‘‘She immediately fit right in. She knew most of the girls from the community and the neighborhood.’’</p><p>And she’ll be a big part of whatever success the Rams have this season.</p><p>‘‘We are guard-driven and guard-loaded,’’ Morgan said. ‘‘Her shooting is going to allow us to stretch the court. We don’t have two 6-2 kids [anymore]. We’re going to try to get<br>after some people.’’</p>

entries.title: Music venue expected to be centerpiece of $7 billion development project near United Center
entries.summary: <p>Details of the new 6,000-seat music venue planned around the United Center as part of a $7 billion privately funded redevelopment project were released on Friday.</p><p>The Music Hall, which is intended to “create a new type of music experience” in Chicago, is scheduled to open in 2028. Its design is meant to center live performances, unlike other Chicago venues, according to a news release.</p><p>Renderings released show a three-level “intimate” performances room, with panoramic stage views and dramatic lighting. The venue is also pictured to have a terrace overlooking the United Center, and dedicated community spaces. Audiences will be able to be seated near the stage to create a unique experience. Retail locations, multiple large bars and a flowing open outdoor space are planned.</p><p>It’s all part of the 1901 Project, an effort aimed at transforming over 55 acres around the United Center into an attractive mixed-use neighborhood. Construction officially <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/03/united-center-owners-wirtz-reinsdorf-break-ground-7-billion-1901-project" target="_blank" ><u>kicked off earlier</u></a> this summer. The Music Hall is an addition to a much larger plan to weave together new developments around the United Center.</p><p>Elected officials have called the project the largest private investment on the entries.title: Sox pitcher Mike Vasil throws for first time since Tommy John surgery
entries.summary: <p>Injured right-hander <b>Mike Vasil</b> has been the White Sox’ most visible, boisterous cheerleader all season.</p><p>Before the Sox’ game Friday against the Tigers, his teammates returned the favor.</p><p>Vasil has been sidelined since spring training after tearing the ulnar collateral ligament in his right elbow in a Cactus League game March 14 and having Tommy John surgery April 2. On Friday, he threw a baseball for the first time since the procedure, making 20 tosses from 45 feet on the left-field grass at Rate Field.</p><p>Vasil has been with the Sox all season during his recovery. He became an online sensation for waving a Harry Potter ‘‘wizard wand’’ and donning a pointed wizard hat to help the team celebrate home runs. The Sox even had a wand giveaway night Sept. 4.</p><p>On Friday, Sox players cycled the magic and love back to Vasil. They introduced him on a speaker system as ‘‘Windy City Wizard, Mike Vasil’’ as he sprung out of the dugout, then gathered around a jumping, delighted Vasil as he loosened up and threw.</p><p>‘‘It felt great,’’ Vasil said. ‘‘Shout-out to Dr. [<b>Keith</b>] <b>Meister</b>. A lot of panic this morning. I was in the shower, and I was slightly concerned about if I remembered how to throw a baseball.’’</p><p>The good vibes were more than mechanical.</p><p>‘‘Overall, to have the support of my teammates, too, it really made me emotional,’’ Vasil said. ‘‘Just the fact everyone is behind me and supporting me. I wanted to pitch this year, and it didn’t happen. But to see them out there meant a lot.’’</p><p>The Sox seemed to be conspiring in the clubhouse before Vasil’s session, but they didn’t tell him any details.</p><p>‘‘I didn’t know that was going to happen,’’ Vasil said. ‘‘It was cool to see all of them.’’</p><p>This would have been Vasil’s second season in the majors after he went 5-3 with a 2.50 ERA in 101 innings in a ‘‘Swiss Army knife’’ role with the 102-loss Sox last season. A healthy Vasil figured to fit in with manager <b>Will Venable’s</b> approach of using pitchers in all types of situations.</p><p>‘‘It’s one of the more fun roles in baseball, being able to either go three [innings] in the middle of the game, close or start on any given day,’’ Vasil said. ‘‘It was so fun last year doing that.’’</p><p>Venable was delighted about Vasil’s milestone day and the players’ response.</p><p>‘‘Really proud of ‘Vas’ for getting to point where he’s out here throwing,’’ Venable said. ‘‘It’s really special when you think about what ‘Vas’ has put into this group and, on a daily basis, the energy that he provides our group.</p><p>‘‘That can kind of take a lot out of you, and you forget that he’s rehabbing from Tommy John surgery, which is a really tough thing to do.’’</p><p>Vasil said he hopes to be throwing rehab assignments by next spring, then be activated in late May. There’s still a lot of work ahead.</p><p>He’ll throw again Sunday, then progress slowly to greater distances.</p><p>‘‘Then eventually get on the mound, start throwing bullpen [sessions],’’ Vasil said. ‘‘That’s the long progression, live at-bats. I’m going to do everything in my power to be back right on time.</p><p>‘‘I want to be better than ever. I know I will be.’’</p><h3>Colson in lineup vs. Tigers</h3><p>Shortstop <b>Colson Montgomery</b> was back in the Sox’ lineup Friday, batting eighth against Tigers left-hander <b>Andrew Sears</b>. He responded by hitting a three-run double in the Sox’ six-run first inning.</p><p>Montgomery was hit on the left wrist by a pitch from the Guardians’ <b>Parker Messick</b> on Wednesday in Cleveland. He left that game after being unable to swing the bat and sat out the Sox’ 3-1 victory Thursday against the Tigers.</p><p>Montgomery entered Friday with three hits in 45 at-bats (54 plate appearances) in his last 14 games, a .067 batting average. Two of the hits were homers and one was a double. He had walked five times and been plunked four times.</p>

entries.title: Losing ugly? Sox blow big early lead and fall to Tigers
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> were rolling and raced to a huge early lead Friday against the Tigers at Rate Field.</p><p>Then their pitching staff, including two of their go-to relievers this season, melted down in an ugly 11-8 loss that dropped them a game behind the first-place Guardians in the American League Central.</p><p>It was another defeat that hurt in the South Siders’ playoff push for a division title or an AL wild card. The Sox, now 78-76, are 6-13 since Aug. 29, when they peaked at nine games above .500 (72-63) with a victory against the Twins in Minnesota.</p><p>The Sox staked rookie right-hander David Sandlin to a 8-2 lead in this one, scoring six runs — all unearned — in the first inning and adding two more on Miguel Vargas’ 32nd home run in the third.</p><p>But Sandlin and the Sox’ bullpen couldn’t hold it.</p><p>‘‘That’s tough, no way about it,’’ manager Will Venable said. ‘‘We obviously have a special first inning there and get the lead. [Then Vargas] with a nice homer. And then, yeah, just weren’t able to get any outs.’’</p><p>The Tigers pulled to 8-5 in the fifth on a bases-loaded triple by Kevin McGonigle. Rookie left-hander Hagen Smith relieved Sandlin, who seemed in control through four innings but suddenly couldn’t get an out.</p><p>‘‘I mean, that’s what you ask for as a starting pitcher,’’ Sandlin said. ‘‘Those guys went to work for me, and I couldn’t go to work for them at the end of the day. That’s on me.</p><p>‘‘I’ve got to get more than four innings as a starter and save the bullpen.’’</p><p>Adding to the pain, All-Star outfielder Tristan Peters — who was playing right — hit the wall hard trying to snare McGonigle’s drive and left the game. He suffered a bruised left shoulder and is day-to-day.</p><p>The Sox’ bullpen certainly didn’t save this one, either. The Tigers narrowed their deficit to 8-6 on an RBI double by Hao-Yu Lee against left-hander Chris Murphy in the sixth, then scored five runs in the eighth on the strength of two-run homers by Lee and Riley Greene.</p><p>Lee smacked a two-run shot to right off left-hander Sean Newcomb’s center-cut high fastball to tie the score 8-8 after Newcomb had hit Eduardo Valencia with a pitch on an 0-2 count.</p><p>Newcomb then walked McGonigle. Left-hander Bryan Hudson entered and yielded two singles that put the Tigers ahead 9-8 before Greene launched his 21st homer to complete the rally.</p><p>Newcomb (2-5) was charged the loss, yielding three runs while getting only two outs. He has been scored on in six of his last seven outings, allowing 12 runs in eight innings, after going 11 appearances without yielding a run.</p><p>Hudson, who has been ultra-reliable this season, allowed two runs and four hits in a third of an inning. He hadn’t been scored on in his 11 previous outings spanning 12⅓ innings.</p><p>‘‘We couldn’t slow them down,’’ Venable said. ‘‘It didn’t really matter what spots we put guys in.’’</p><p>After the game, Peters said he ‘‘felt all right and better than initially’’ but was ‘‘really sore.’’ He said the impact from hitting the right-center wall affected ‘‘the back of my shoulder and kind of crunched by shoulders forward.’’</p><p>‘‘I’ve always been a guy that’s going to run into the wall and try to make plays,’’ he said.</p>

entries.title: Michael Busch's caught-stealing caps Cubs' frustrating loss to Reds
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — Outside of Wrigley Field, Cubs left fielder Ian Happ is most productive at Great American Ballpark. He entered the game Friday against the Reds with 18 home runs and a 1.002 OPS there, his best marks at an opponent’s park.</p><p>He added a homer in the third inning, giving him the sixth-most by a visiting player in the stadium’s 24-year history. So why on earth did Michael Busch, who had reached on a walk in the ninth inning, try stealing second base with two outs and Happ representing the tying run?</p><p>After being called safe, Busch was ruled out on a video review, and the Cubs lost 6-4.</p><p>“That was a dumb play,” manager Craig Counsell said. “It was stupid. I’ll take responsibility for it.”</p><p>“That’s just inexcusable on my part,” Busch said. “Gotta make sure if I’m taking that base that I make it 100%. We have a good hitter up in Happ, and that can’t happen.”</p><p>It wasn’t one of the biggest reasons the Cubs lost. Those were right-hander Clay Holmes walking five — including three in the Reds’ game-turning three-run sixth — and the hitters going 2-for-10 with runners in scoring position and leaving nine men on base overall.</p><p>“Can’t walk the leadoff guy there in the sixth inning,” Holmes said. “The walks hurt. The past three outings, I haven’t been efficient.”</p><p>Fortunately for the Cubs, the Phillies also lost, keeping the teams tied for the top spot in the National League wild-card race, with the Cubs holding the tiebreaker. Unfortunately for them, the Padres had a chance to make it a three-way tie late Friday.</p><h3>Swanson returns to action</h3><p>After a rehab assignment that never happened and two simulated games, shortstop Dansby Swanson returned from a strained left oblique. He looked no worse for wear from the start.</p><p>Reds leadoff man Carlos Jorge hit a pop fly down the third-base line that Swanson chased all the way into foul territory next to short left field. He slid on the warning track as he neared the wall but couldn’t make the catch. The official scorer ruled it no play, but that couldn’t have been further from the truth.</p><p>If anyone had concerns about how Swanson’s body would react to real game action, that play should’ve allayed those fears.</p><p>Swanson missed a month with the injury, and his rehab assignment this week with Triple-A Iowa got rained out, forcing the Cubs to get creative. They flew in two minor-leaguers to pitch to him in a sim game Wednesday, during which Swanson also played in the field. He got in another workout Thursday at Wrigley Field before the team left town.</p><p>“We’re our best team when Dansby’s out there,” Counsell said. “We’re our best defensive unit, for sure. The rehab part got screwed up with the weather. We’re excited to have him back.”</p><p>Swanson batted ninth, going 1-for-3 with a walk and a run scored. His hit was an infield single on which he beat the throw from Elly De La Cruz deep in the hole at short.</p><h3>Playoff rotation can wait</h3><p>With only eight games left in the regular season after Friday and a playoff berth likely in their future, the Cubs are starting to think about how they’d like to line up their postseason rotation. But thinking is all that they’re doing.</p><p>“We’ve got a lot to accomplish before that,” Counsell said. “Do you start thinking about those things? Absolutely, you have to think about them. But my experience is that those decisions change many times. So you just kind of position yourself for possibilities.”</p><p>Counsell refuses to look at much beyond the game at hand.</p><p>“Worry about today; that’s all we can do today,” he said. “I know that’s coachspeak, but it’s how you have to work as athletes and coaches. Getting ahead of ourselves for those things is useless.”</p>

entries.title: Welch, state Democrats offer different accounts of campaign funding dispute
entries.summary: <p>My associate Isabel Miller and I told subscribers earlier this month that Democrats for the Illinois House had been suddenly cut off from the Democratic Party of Illinois’ lucrative postage discount program, which can save as much as one-third to half of campaign postage costs.</p><p>Afterward, an extraordinary interaction occurred between the executive director of the House Democrats’ caucus campaign committee and the chair of the Democratic Party of Illinois.</p><p>Let’s first break down a few differences in the two stories offered in separate explanatory emails sent to House Democrats.</p><p>Democrats for the Illinois House’s TaQuoya McConnico explained the decision to walk away from the state party this way: “The financial structure proposed for participation in the coordinated campaign called for a $750,000 investment followed by an adjusted $500,000 investment that demanded a payment from each individual House member – YOU. Speaker declined to commit to payment from each House member.”</p><p>This unprecedented action to split from the Democratic Party of Illinois was taken less than two months before Election Day without Illinois House Speaker Emanuel "Chris" Welch ever consulting members of his House Democratic Caucus. </p><p>Welch has been under fire for months for how he has run the chamber, to the point where it’s no longer a slam dunk that he will be reelected in January. Cutting out your members before taking such a late-in-the-game step probably isn’t helping his cause.</p><p>State Democratic Party of Illinois Chair Lisa Hernandez told House Democrats hours later that the party had reduced its ask twice — ultimately requesting just $400,000 — “the same contribution as the Senate,” which has about half the number of members as the House and far fewer targeted races on the ballot. That’s a pretty good deal.</p><p>But the offer was still rejected, and for questionable reasons. “The proposed DPI-coordinated campaign structure called for Welch to demand $10,000 in contributions from every single House member — even in cases where members don’t have a race and don’t have that amount of cash on hand,” McConnico wrote, giving the above-mentioned total of $500,000.</p><p>Hernandez told a much different story.</p><p> “We did not demand that individual members personally write $10,000 checks to DPI. I asked members to help raise those funds, and I offered to make those fundraising calls myself.</p><p>"The $10,000 reflects federal limits on Levin funds, which help fund voter registration, voter contact, and get-out-the-vote work through the Coordinated Campaign. Because those funds are limited to $10,000 from any one source, funding an operation of this size requires support from multiple contributors. I wanted to do whatever I could to help us reach an agreement.”</p><p>There’s a school of thought that Welch didn’t want to ask some of his members to pony up $10,000 each (even with state party help) to buy them into the party’s coordinated campaign when, as mentioned above, several of his members are refusing to give him another term with the gavel. </p><p>And the Welch allies may somehow see the hand of Gov. JB Pritzker in all this because Pritzker has not explicitly defended Welch during successive scandals this summer.</p><p>A House Democratic official told another publication last week that Welch is also more concerned that a coordinated campaign would benefit the top of the ticket far more than legislative candidates.</p><p>But the object of some past coordinated campaign mailers has been to use the popularity of the top of the ticket to boost legislative and down-ballot candidates.</p><p>Welch also demanded a $2.1 million refund from the state party, which the party, in a spirit of cooperation, complied with immediately. The money hadn’t yet been spent on direct mail.</p><p>Welch also demanded that the party comb through its files to determine whether he was owed a refund on another $2 million already given to DPI and mostly spent on mail. The state party spent last week working with its campaign vendors to look for any possible Welch money when it should’ve been working on its fall campaign operation.</p><p>McConnico said in her letter to members that it was possible that Welch would push for a special meeting of the state party to discuss the rift. But sources said Welch didn’t have enough weighted votes to get the meeting called, especially with the clock ticking toward November.</p><p>This is no way to run a rodeo.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bc0000" name="module-bc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Can Blackhawks goalie Spencer Knight repeat excellence in hockey's most variable position?
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks?_gl=1*18p3uw7*_up*MQ..*_ga*NjIxMDIzMjM4LjE3ODk3NjgzMjI.*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODk3NjgzMjEkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODk3NjgzMjEkajYwJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> goalie Spencer Knight's breakout was, from a long-term perspective, arguably the best and most important thing that happened around the organization last season.</p><p>Can he repeat it?</p><p>Most fans seem to be taking it for granted that he will, because there's no reason to believe he won't. Knight was long forecast to become one of the league's best goalies one day, and at age 25, he's just entering his prime.</p><p>He's extremely technically sound, and that — combined with his overall athleticism and lower-body flexibility and explosiveness — allows him to excel at making high-danger saves in particular. That pattern dates back to his Panthers tenure.</p><p>He's also disciplined off the ice, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2025/11/30/blackhawks-nhl-goalie-spencer-knight-off-ice-habits-red-light-mat" >wowing teammates</a> with a relentless pursuit of strategies to maximize his nutrition, rest and recovery. He checks every box that an elite goalie should check.</p><p>But goaltending is difficult, and aside from a few ultra-elite goalies, goalie performance tends to fluctuate significantly from year to year. In that way, goalies are more like MLB relief pitchers than their NHL forward and defensemen teammates.</p><p>Knight bailed out the Hawks' leaky defense and opened eyes around the league with a +10.5 GSAA last season (per Natural Stat Trick), which essentially means he allowed 10.5 fewer goals against than an average goalie facing the same quantity and quality of shots would. He was one of 17 goalies who posted GSAAs over 10.</p><p>That doesn't guarantee he'll remain in that statistical upper tier again this season, though. In fact, looking through recent history, the odds are he won't.</p><p>Of the 14 goalies who posted GSAAs over 10 in 2024-25, only five did so again in 2025-26: Andrei Vasilevskiy (Lightning), Filip Gustavsson (Wild), Jet Greaves (Blue Jackets), Logan Thompson (Capitals) and Ilya Sorokin (Islanders).</p><p>Five others posted GSAAs between 0 and 10, and four posted negative GSAAs, meaning they entries.title: Meta — and parents — share responsibility in curbing social media addiction
entries.summary: <p>Parenting. That was my first thought when I learned about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/technology/2026/08/26/meta-illinois-pay-nearly-768-million-multistate-settlement-teen-social-media-addiction" >Meta’s settlement</a> of allegations that both Facebook and Instagram harmed young teenagers by contributing to social media addiction. </p><p>I agree that Meta should absolutely be held accountable for how its apps are purposely designed to appeal to a younger audience. But I also think that there is another major factor alongside an app's design: parenting.</p><p>In my AP Psychology class, I learned about nature (genes) and nurture (environment). Our behavior is influenced not just by our genes, but also by the environments around us. Smartphones can provide comfort, entertainment and community, but they cannot shape the environment where teenagers use them. That is the parent's responsibility.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/sections/shots-health-news/2024/06/08/nx-s1-4993778/give-yourself-your-kids-break-from-screen-time-guilt" target="_blank" >2024 study</a> of more than 10,000 12- and 13-year-olds, and their parents found that parental monitoring and reasonable limits on screen use were associated with lower screen time and less problematic social-media use (Pediatric Research, 2024). </p><p>This conclusion does not mean that parents should constantly invade their children's privacy to protect them. It means that they must have regular conversations with their child about what they experience online.</p><p>To reiterate, I am not calling for an act to sue parents (that is just silly), but I am calling for greater public emphasis that they must be involved in protecting their children online. Meta must be accountable for its products. </p><p>Parents must be accountable for parenting. Protecting teenagers online will require both.</p><p><i>Rhea Mae Bayan, Lane Technical High School</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a90001" name="module-a90001"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Use Flock responsibly</h3><p>Cities, towns and colleges around the country are cutting ties with the controversial surveillance technology company Flock Safety. One of the major concerns is privacy and safety.</p><p>Keep in mind that if you are on a public way or expressway, you do not have a reasonable expectation of privacy. That being said, if a police officer uses Flock for nefarious purposes, that officer should be charged and/or terminated.</p><p>Flock claims it's made changes to police forces to limit who can access the camera data. If those changes aren’t enough, then cancel the Flock contract. If used properly, Flock is a good crime-fighting tool for law enforcement. The data collected should not be stored forever.</p><p>Law enforcement agencies need to have strict guidelines on how any information is accessed on Flock, so it’s used only for investigative purposes only.</p><p><i>Richard Barber, Mount Greenwood</i></p><h3>Release video gambling licenses</h3><p>Across Chicago, small businesses are struggling to remain open amid rising operating costs and razor-thin profit margins. </p><p>This challenge is especially serious in North Lawndale, a community that has historically received less economic investment than many other neighborhoods. Nevertheless, our dedicated entrepreneurs continue seeking opportunities to grow, create jobs and serve the community.</p><p>As president and CEO of the Chi North Lawndale Chamber of Commerce, it is my responsibility to advocate for practical resources that can help these businesses succeed.</p><p>When the Chicago City Council <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/09/16/video-gaming-in-chicago-proposal-anthony-beale-brandon-johnson" >authorized video gambling terminals</a>, commonly known as VGTs, neighborhood restaurant and bar owners hoped the machines would provide supplemental revenue to help cover payroll, taxes, utilities, maintenance and other operating expenses. </p><p>However, qualified <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/casinos-gambling/2026/06/19/chicago-video-gambling-machines-vgt-bars-restaurants" >establishments are still waiting</a> for the city’s licensing process to move forward.</p><p>For businesses in North Lawndale, this delay has serious financial consequences. Many establishments are already operating under significant pressure, and continued uncertainty makes it harder for them to plan, retain employees and keep their doors open.</p><p>VGT revenue could serve as a form of "economic gap insurance" — helping eligible businesses withstand rising costs, preserve neighborhood jobs and remain rooted in the communities they helped build.</p><p>We respectfully urge the Chicago Department of Business Affairs and Consumer Protection to move forward without further delay, establish a clear and transparent implementation process, and begin reviewing and issuing licenses to qualified establishments.</p><p>Chicago should ensure that neighborhood businesses have equitable access to the economic opportunities authorized by the City Council. Protecting the interests of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/09/ballys-permanent-casino-river-west-construction-slowdown-video-gambling-terminals-city-council-license-committee" >major casino operator</a> should not come at the expense of the small restaurants and bars that employ local residents, contribute to neighborhood corridors and serve Chicago communities every day.</p><p>It is time to support our local businesses and move the VGT licensing process forward.</p><p><i>Denita Sanders, Chi North Lawndale Chamber of Commerce</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Tensions Rise After Workplace Romance Breakup
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a man in my 40s. A woman and I had a relationship that ended badly. We met on the job, though we work in different departments. Everyone knows about our previous relationship, and it is extremely awkward. Every time I walk by, there are lots of smiles and chattering; when I approach my co-workers' desks, I'm greeted with silence and intense stares. I still have strong feelings for her, and I know they are reciprocated because she has verbalized it and shown it with her actions and behaviors.</p><p>After she ended things, I was upset and gave her the silent treatment. I know she feels hurt by my pretending like she doesn't exist. I am a stubborn man, but I really miss her. After the breakup, she mentioned being friends. I cannot be friends with her. Despite the amount of time that has gone by, I still want to fix things. However, I know my real intentions and illusions about getting back together are misguided fantasy. I would appreciate your insights. — <i>AWKWARD AT WORK</i></p><p><b>DEAR AWKWARD:</b> Do you understand that it's you, not your co-workers, making things awkward? By resorting to the silent treatment, you've made everyone uncomfortable. You say you want to fix things, but you've made no attempt to do so. You don't believe you can reconcile with your ex, but on what grounds? You won't even talk to her!</p><p>I don't think you're "stubborn"; I think you're afraid. You've kept up this unseemly behavior because you don't want to be hurt again. If you can't muster the courage to tell this woman you want another chance, you have two options left: Either speak with her purely as a colleague and bury the hatchet so you can at least be cordial in the workplace, or start looking for another job.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My father's girlfriend, "Jane," has started soliciting money for her causes from everyone she knows, especially our family members. After the first request, I donated a modest amount to support her, not knowing the deluge of requests that would follow. I have a set amount of money I can use for charity and would rather decide for myself how to spend it.</p><p>Jane and my father are sensitive about her being accepted into our family. They both tend to look for slights and then blow them out of proportion. Dad has made it clear that unless my siblings and I fully embrace Jane, he won't be part of our lives. I admire him sticking up for her, but I know if I decline the next donation request it's going to get ugly. I feel like I'm being held hostage. How do I get out of this situation? — <i>HELD HOSTAGE IN VANCOUVER</i></p><p><b>DEAR HELD HOSTAGE:</b> Talk to your father privately and tell him you love him. Remind him that you don't have an unlimited amount of money to donate to charity, that you have causes of your own that are important to you, and that you have already donated to Jane's more than once. Ask him to explain that to her and that it isn't a rejection of her — just fiscal responsibility on your part. He needs to know you feel like you won't be able to have a relationship with the father you adore if you refuse these solicitations.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: From a WWII drone to cargo pants, a Lake View military surplus store marks 80 years in business
entries.summary: <p>Adam Hirsch has a favorite phrase about the industry his family has been in for 80 years.</p><p>“When the country goes to hell, we do well,” he said.</p><p>Hirsch, 42, took over the Lake View store Army Navy Sales from his father in 2012, returning to his hometown from Los Angeles, where he was a television producer.</p><p>Now, he spends his days in the store — clad in an Army Navy Sales T-shirt — sorting through a seemingly endless inventory of military surplus goods.</p><p>This year, the business, at 3100 N. Lincoln Ave., which touts itself as the last authentic military surplus store in Chicago, marks its 80th anniversary.</p><p>The surplus industry stems from the excess military goods following World War II, when entrepreneurs began buying items in bulk from the government to resell to the public. But the business isn’t as popular as it once was, Hirsch said.</p><p>“A lot of young people don't know what surplus is. A lot of young people want to buy brands,” he said. “They want to buy Patagonia. They want to buy North Face. What we sell is government surplus, so it's not really branded stuff. It's stuff that the government made, but it's very high-quality, American-made stuff.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: What do you think about City Council's potential new parking meter deal? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked readers what they think about the City Council's potential new parking meter deal. Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>“It's great that the old parking deal is evolving, but it's difficult to square ‘lucrative benefits for the city and motorists’ with important city goals to improve living conditions and reduce costs by moving away from private car travel."<br><i>— Melanie Eckner</i></p><p>“I think it stops some of the bleeding from when they take the spots out of service. Hire a dedicated person that coordinates the departments to make sure those spots are put back in service ASAP. Make sure the utility companies pay for spots they leave out of service.” <br><i>— Dean R. Martin</i></p><p>“I’m really impressed with the gains made by the City Council team. Actually, I’m shocked! Could it be that government can be functional? The original deal has been an albatross, so any improvement is welcome. The fact that City Council members got together to negotiate a decent outcome is to be applauded.”<br><i>— Kathleen Alaimo</i></p><p>“Tired of deals the city makes. entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Visual Journalist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/candace-chambers" target="_blank" >Candace Dane Chambers</a>.</p><h3>What makes this photo important?</h3><p>Actress Keke Palmer is a Robbins native whose star has steadily risen since she burst into the Hollywood scene with 2006's "Akeelah and the Bee." entries.summary: <p>“She’s a genius.”</p><p>“She’s gonna be famous one day.”</p><p>This was the chatter among audiences who gathered inside the theater this week at the <a class="Link" href="https://www.gertie.co/" target="_blank" ><u>Gertie Hub</u></a>, 400 N. Peoria, to see <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/trophysophie/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>Sophie Becker</u></a> perform with her ventriloquist dummy, Ronnie Woods.</p><p>Throughout the act, the pair were singing, swapping voices, creating sound effects and more.</p><p>The production, part of a show called “82 Nights Only,” was one of several events happening around the kickoff week for <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoexhibitionweek.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Exhibition Week</u></a>. Happening through Sunday, the event — organized by Chicago contemporary art platform Gertie — spotlights more than 40 art galleries and creative institutions. </p><p>Many of the affiliated galleries have set up new shows that are visible through the fall, and others through next year. (Click here for our gallery guide of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/art/2026/09/14/art-gallery-guide-chicago-exhibition-week-galleries-west-loop-contemporary" target="_blank" ><u>10 local art shows</u></a> to see this fall.)</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2a0000" name="image-2a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ae12be4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7309x4102+0+387/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9b%2F9f%2F620aa25540e5acd151352e115e4f%2F2026-09-16-gertie-performances-77.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/102ed38/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7309x4102+0+387/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9b%2F9f%2F620aa25540e5acd151352e115e4f%2F2026-09-16-gertie-performances-77.jpeg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3a8e9ee/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7309x4102+0+387/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9b%2F9f%2F620aa25540e5acd151352e115e4f%2F2026-09-16-gertie-performances-77.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ventriloquist Sophie Becker performs at the Gertie Hub, 400 N. The exhibition week is meant to attract old and new art lovers and collectors and poke fun at the often stuffy and unwelcoming gallery culture.</p><p>“What we're trying to do is offer a couple of different on-ramps to people,” said Abby Pucker, the founder of Gertie, who is incentivizing those who visit at least four galleries to collect stickers from each and get free admission to the Museum of Contemporary Art on Sunday. “My ask to people actually is to get up and go do stuff. Be in the world and use it as an opportunity to invite friends.”</p><p>Running through Dec. 13, “82 Nights Only” features a rotating array of artists' work and performances. entries.summary: <h3><b>WHEN THE </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" ><b>BEARS</b></a><b> HAVE THE BALL</b></h3><p> <br>What makes the chess match between Ben Johnson and Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores is so compelling is how similar their complaints are about each other’s system. Johnson can be run-heavy one week and pass-happy the next, while Flores could blitz from all over the field — or, as he did in Week 1 last year, barely at all. Flores’ ability so shift tendencies is reminiscent of his mentor Bill Belichick, whom Johnson often cites as one of his favorites.</p><p>Both coordinators spent the week trying to give their players answers — both before and after the snap. The Bears, though, don’t often like to gives Flores that much time at the line of scrimmage. The Bears snapped the ball quickly more often against the Vikings than any other team last year, per ESPN. That gave the Vikings less time to communicate with each other — and to figure out Johnson’s formations and personnel groupings.</p><p>Edge rusher Dallas Turner led the NFL in pass rush win rate in Week 1. Ben Johnson singled out another player, defensive end Jalen Redmond, as one of the best in the league and veteran safety Harrison Smith, who played 38% of the snaps last week as he works his way back into shape, as a coordinator on the field.</p><p>Quarterback Caleb Williams has avoided mistakes against Flores. In four games, he’s thrown four touchdowns and no interceptions, good for a 88.1 passer rating. He was sacked nine times. Johnson likely won’t be content with more of the same — Williams needs to not only protect the ball against Flores, but be productive.</p><h3><b>WHEN THE </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/09/17/bears-vikings-podcast-caleb-williams" target="_blank" ><b>VIKINGS</b></a><b> HAVE THE BALL</b></h3><p>The Vikings’ season opening win against the Packers came at a cost — starting quarterback Kyler Murray was concussed in the first quarter and leading rusher Jordan Mason hurt his thumb, requiring surgery and a trip to injured reserve.</p><p>Carson Wentz, who helped rally the Vikings to the final 29 points against the Packers, will start Sunday. He is 4-0 career against the Bears. In his last start at Soldier Field, though, Wentz threw for just 99 yards in a 12-9 Commanders win in 2022.</p><p>He’ll has plenty of weapons to rely on, starting with receivers Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison. Jefferson has 790 receiving yards against the Bears since he came into the league in 2020, the most of any Bears opponent. Since Addison was drafted in 2023, he actually has 107 more receiving yards against the Bears than Jefferson does. Addison ran 28 routes last week, the second-most on the team, but didn’t catch either of the two passes thrown his way.</p><p>Cornerbacks Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson will be humiliated if they play the same way they did last week.
